# Draft:Portugal and Its Colonial Legacy: History, Memory, and Decolonisation

Decolonising Portugal
The history and memory of the Portuguese colonial past are central to its national identity. This is evident in the emphasis on the imperial theme found in the national flag, anthem, history curricula, and even the memorial landscapes of its cities.. The Portuguese empire was not only the first European empire but also the last and longest-lasting, spanning more than five centuries. This extensive history has significantly influenced Portuguese nationalism and how it is popularly disseminated File:Https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f4/PortugueseColonialEmpire02.png
Much like Britain, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, Portugal was at the centre of a colonial empire that exploited territories beyond its European borders. However, despite these similarities, each colonial power—Portugal included—possessed its own distinct national and imperial characteristics (Albrecht, 2017).
Portugal, through an agreement known as the Portuguese Padroado with the Catholic Church, was granted exclusive authority over religious activities in its “discovered” lands, hence why the nation’s elites have often equated colonisation with Christianisation. Despite this framing, Portugal, like its European counterparts, employed extreme violence and exploitation in its colonial ventures . It actively promoted and practiced the slave trade and slavery , maintained forced labor well into the post-Second World War era , and enforced segregation based on racist criteria .
National Pride
Portugal’s colonial past has long been framed as a source of national pride, particularly through the glorification of the Age of Discoveries  in history books, public monuments, and political discourse. Historians and scholars often portray the nation's maritime expansion as a defining moment of national identity, emphasising the country's role in global exploration rather than its colonial domination. Education and cultural memory also reinforce this narrative, where Portuguese explorers are depicted as pioneers of globalisation, omitting the violence of colonial rule, forced and the transatlantic slave trade . The term Saudade, a uniquely Portuguese concept signifying nostalgic longing, plays a role in this colonial memory, fostering a sentimental attachment to the empire rather than a critical view of its legacy. Scholars argue that this nostalgia contributes to colonial amnesia, preventing meaningful confrontation with historical wrongdoings.
Spillover effects and Nostalgia
Portugal’s colonial history continues to have a long-lasting effect on contemporary society, shaping political decisions, demographics and cultural narratives. Lusotropicalism, developed by sociologist Gilberto Freye, is a theory that portrays Portuguese colonialism as inherently friendly and racially inclusive, all while downplaying the realities of exploitation, violence and forced labor. This ideology continues to influence many Portuguese people’s views on their country’s colonial past, regardless of it having been challenged by scholars.
This phenomenon reflects on today’s society in numerous ways; Despite being a part of the European Union, the country frequently makes remarks towards its “historical relationships” with its former colonies, in order to strengthen its international standing, revealing an identity struggle for the nation after the loss of its empires, looking back at the colonial period with nostalgia. Although the country has embraced its European identity, it also aims to distinguish itself from other EU Member States by capitalising on its historical ties with Lusophone Africa and Brazil. besides that, Portugal continues to maintain and exert economic influence in the continent of Africa, particularly in countries like Mozambique and Angola, where Portuguese companies are in dominant positions in sectors such as energy, construction, and banking.

The Community of Portuguese Language Countries (CPLP) established in 1996, is a cultural and political organisation with the primary purpose of bridging Portugal with its former colonies, all while promoting cultural and linguistic partnership. Critics have been labelling the CPLP’s acts as neo-imperial, with the underlying goal of retaining control in the Lusophone world.
As far as demographics and urban layouts are concerned, there are noticeable immigration and racial segregation patterns. The African presence in Portugal, particularly Lisbon, has old and historical roots. Estimates indicate that Africans made up 10% of the city’s population during the 16th century, leading to current trends of racial segregation. nowadays, white Portuguese people are typically concentrated in city centers, while racialised populations, many times immigrants or their descendants from former colonies, are more commonly found living in peripheral neighborhoods. Today, around 782,000 immigrants reside lawfully in Portugal, accounting for 7% of the overall population. Many of these immigrants come from former Portuguese colonies, such as Brazil, Cape Verde and Angola. These descendants of ex colonies’ migrants face economic discrimination and struggles, reconfirming the marginalisation of Afro-descendant communities in Portugal.
Bottom-Up Reckoning
In recent years, bottom-up movements have sought to challenge the dominant narrative of Portuguese colonial history. A recent incident was the vandalisation of the Padre António Vieira statue in Lisbon during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, with protesters defacing the statue, writing the word “decolonise” at its base, and painting the depicted children with red hearts. Another significant example of community led movements is the initiative by Djass Association of Afro-Descendants, called ‘Memorial to the victims of slavery in Lisbon’. The grassroot organisation initiated a public memorial in hopes of the recognition of the role of Portugal in the transatlantic slave trade and mourn its victimsGolemo, Karolina. 2023. “Decolonising Memory and Spaces: Contemporary Narratives about Portugal’s Colonising Past”. Politeja 20 (3(84):19-30. . The design was developed by an Angolan artist, Kiluanji Kia Henda, and it was chosen by public voting procedures. The project was given the title “Plantation - Prosperity and nightmare” and it depicted a sugar cane plantation. However, the 2021 mayoral transfer to a center-right administration ended up delaying its installation, reinforcing concerns that the local government is blocking efforts to acknowledge the country’s colonial pastGolemo, Karolina. 2023. “Decolonising Memory and Spaces: Contemporary Narratives about Portugal’s Colonising Past”. Politeja 20 (3(84):19-30.  .
Top-Down Initiatives

Scholars have described the reluctance of former colonial powers to fully engage with their colonial past as ‘post-colonial amnesia’  or ‘colonial aphasia’ . These terms denote an official approach to colonial history that either erases it completely or presents a selective version, emphasising its so-called positive aspects while omitting the violence and exploitation it entailed. Portugal is no exception to this trend. After the fall of the dictatorship and the end of colonial rule, the Portuguese state gradually dismissed transitional justice concerning the dictatorship's crimes and entirely disregarded accountability for colonial-era atrocities. In the 1970s, measures such as purges, trials, truth commissions, compensation, and amnesties were introduced to address the dictatorial past, but no comparable mechanisms were established for reckoning with colonialism .
A significant shift occurred in 2022 when Portuguese Prime Minister Minister António Costa, during a visit to Maputo, formally apologised to Mozambique’s president for the 1972 Wiriyamu massacre, in which the Portuguese military killed approximately 400 unarmed civilians. This marked the first official recognition of a colonial-era crime by a Portuguese leader. However, Costa emphasised that these atrocities occurred under the dictatorship, implying that its downfall ‘opened the door to peace’ and situating colonial violence within the broader context of Portugal’s authoritarian past.
Building upon this, President Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa in his speech on April 25, 2023 in the national Parliament during the annual commemoration of the Carnation Revolution, he called for Portugal to apologise to its former colonies for the exploitation and slavery they endured. He also highlighted what he saw as its positive legacies, such as the spread of the Portuguese language and culture. In doing so, Rebelo de Sousa attempted to balance historical accountability while emphasising on post-imperial cultural ties. At a time of shifting global power dynamics, these official apologies serve as a form of soft power, aimed at strengthening diplomatic relations .
The Portuguese state has yet to pursue other initiatives for post-colonial justice and reconciliation. Instead, official cultural projects continue to reinforce a nationalistic interpretation of Portugal’s imperial history. Portuguese textbooks emphasise themes of trade and cultural exchange while downplaying or entirely omitting the violence and racial segregation that characterised Portuguese colonial rule . Investigative journalist  Joana Gorjão Henriques  has extensively documented this phenomenon, demonstrating the stark contrast between official narratives that promote the myth of Portuguese non-racism and the enduring realities of institutional and everyday racism in Portugal today  Another case in point is the renovation of Praça do Império  (Empire Square) in Lisbon. The square featured floral arrangements representing the coats of arms of Portugal’s metropolitan and colonial provinces. In 2016, the Lisbon City Council proposed a renovation to make the site more attractive to tourists, which included removing these coats of arms—primarily for practical rather than ideological reasons. .
Ongoing Debates
Portugal continues its reflections and debating its colonial legacy. In April 2024, Portuguese President Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa recognised Portugal's historical responsibility for transatlantic slavery and colonialism. He advocated for finding means to compensate past colonies, such as debt cancellation or special cooperation projects.  Despite the President's speech, the national government has made it clear that it does not intend to offer reparations for the nation's role in slavery and colonialism. The administration stressed its commitment to "strengthening mutual relations, respecting historical truth, and fostering "Deeper and closer cooperation".
While there is a growing worldwide pressure on states to address historical injustices through remedies, Portugal, has been rejecting calls for immediate financial compensation. At the same time, Scholars continue to investigate the long-lasting effects of the nation’s colonial past on modern society. Research areas include the memorialisation of empire, the experiences of settlers who returned to Portugal after the colonies gained their independence, and the way nationalist, colonial-era ideologies continue to shape the country’s identity today .
Counter Movements
Despite the persistence of colonial nostalgia, counter-movements have emerged to challenge the dominant narrative and call for a more critical reassessment of Portugal’s past. Scholars, activists, and Afro-descendant communities have increasingly demanded recognition of colonial injustices, particularly regarding Portugal’s role in the transatlantic slave trade . Public debates have also arisen over colonial-era cultural institutions that continue to celebrate Portugal’s imperial past without critical engagement. For example, while Lisbon’s Museum of Ancient Art (Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga) houses a vast collection of colonial artefacts, it has been criticised for failing to contextualise them within histories of exploitation .
The role of colonial memory in tourism could also be seen as problematic. Sites like Belém, a historic district in Lisbon known for its maritime monuments, and the Monastery of Jerónimos, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built during Portugal’s colonial expansion, continue to attract visitors with little acknowledgment of the suffering caused by colonial expansion. While these locations highlight Portugal’s achievements, critics argue that they do not adequately engage with the consequences of empire, such as forced labor and the displacement of indigenous peoples . furthermore, discussions continue over whether institutions such as the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation, a major cultural and philanthropic organisation, should contribute more actively to post-colonial dialogue and reparative justice . The foundation, established by Armenian oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian, has historically promoted Portuguese cultural heritage but has faced criticism for not adequately addressing colonial legacies in its programming.
Portugal’s approach to its colonial past remains deeply contested, reflecting broader tensions between historical nostalgia and postcolonial reckoning. While national narratives continue to emphasise Portugal’s maritime achievements, counter-movements are gradually pushing for a more inclusive and critical engagement with history
